title: Regulated Delivery, Platforms & Packaging
scopeHtml: Scope: constraint-driven delivery routes (privilege, HIPAA, GDPR, FedRAMP), requirements, lifecycle, platform choice, version pinning, trust boundaries, accelerators and upstream contribution.

notes.title: Constraints pick the route
notes.html:
The principle. If your data must be handled under specific constraints (attorney-client privilege, HIPAA, GDPR, FedRAMP, an internal data-residency policy), that constraint decides which endpoint your code calls, which credentials it carries, and where its logs land — before you make any design choice about prompts, tools or memory. As a developer you usually don't pick the surface, but you write the code that targets an endpoint, attaches credentials, configures the region and emits logs. The wrong client configuration is far more expensive to undo after the agent is wired than to set correctly at the start.

The five constraints.

Constraint What it rules out in code What usually survives review
Attorney-client privilege calls from a consumer-grade Claude.ai surface the firm can't audit end to end; any path sending privileged content to an endpoint the firm hasn't approved, however the prompt is structured direct API/SDK calls from the firm's own application, authenticated via SSO, routed through a firm-approved LLM gateway with full request/response logging. Anthropic's native conversation content (prompts, responses, tool payloads) is not captured by Anthropic by default on direct API traffic, so the organization must implement conversation logging in the application layer and route it to an approved destination; tool calls and results stay in the audited path. Confirm the final design with the Anthropic account team.
HIPAA (PHI) sending PHI to any endpoint or route not covered by a Business Associate Agreement for the specific configuration; any logging/retention path not scoped under the same BAA direct API/SDK on a BAA-covered configuration (coverage for first-party API access is arranged with Anthropic, which provisions a dedicated HIPAA-enabled organization), or a cloud-mediated route via AWS Bedrock or GCP Vertex on the partner's existing HIPAA-eligible account. The BAA does not cover Console, Workbench, beta features or consumer plans; not all API features are covered, so check the current feature-eligibility list before configuring
GDPR / EU data residency routes where the region of model execution can't be pinned in code; defaulting to a global endpoint with no region (the common failure) a cloud-mediated route (Bedrock or Vertex) with the region pinned in client configuration to a covered jurisdiction. The direct Anthropic API does not currently provide EU data residency, so EU-residency partners should route through Bedrock or Vertex
FedRAMP / government any code path calling an endpoint not on an authorized environment at the required impact level — including dev/test paths hitting the commercial endpoint while production hits the authorized one, because credentials and code patterns leak between them three routes as of publication: Claude for Government (FedRAMP High, held through Palantir Federal Cloud Service – Supporting Services), Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud (FedRAMP High and DoD IL4/5), Claude via Vertex AI Assured Workloads (FedRAMP authorized). Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is not FedRAMP authorized. Verify current status at trust.anthropic.com
Internal data-residency policy calls from any SDK client configured against a cloud vendor outside the approved list, regardless of technical capability — procurement rules out the path before engineering preferences the delivery route on the partner's approved vendor: whichever SDK client and endpoint configuration their CIO already cleared; build against it rather than switching mid-project

Managed Agents and regulated work. Sessions are stored server-side, so they are not eligible for ZDR or a BAA; a PHI/ZDR workload rules that wiring path out.

SOC 2. Governs how your systems are built and operated rather than which endpoint your code calls; it belongs with security posture and audit requirements.

Real life. Shipping food across borders: the destination country's rules decide the packaging, route and paperwork, not your preferences.

Tech. Data-residency flags and region settings in a cloud configuration.

notes.title: Requirements and lifecycle
notes.html:
From business problem to requirements. Before any platform is chosen, turn the business problem into checkable requirements.

  • Functional requirements: what the system must do (inputs, outputs, behaviours, acceptance criteria).
  • Infrastructure requirements (derived): residency and region, identity and access, latency, volume, availability, logging and retention, cost ceiling, integration points.
  • Document them so a decision can be defended: why this platform, which constraint drove it. Eliciting infrastructure constraints up front takes a scoping conversation teams are tempted to skip.

The systems lifecycle applied to a Claude application. A Claude application moves through the same lifecycle as any engineered system, with the model work mapped onto it: requirements and design (the design document), build, test and evaluate (evals, test levels), deploy (platform, version pinning), operate and monitor (observability, cost, security), maintain and retire (upgrades, deprecation). The phases are the ones the earlier modules taught one at a time; naming them as a lifecycle shows how they connect.

Each phase needs an artifact and a gate. For example: requirements document → sign-off; design document → review; eval results → ship/no-ship; deployment manifest (pinned versions) → release approval; runbook and dashboards → go-live. Gating between phases adds checkpoints a team under deadline is tempted to skip — and skipping them is the usual failure.

Placing work in the right phase. Success criteria and trust boundaries belong to design; evals to test; pinning and platform to deploy; cost, drift and incident response to operate.

Real life. A building permit process: plans approved before foundations, inspection before occupancy.

Tech. Stage gates in a CI/CD pipeline.

notes.title: Platforms and version pinning
notes.html:
The customer's cloud usually determines the platform. Claude is reachable through the first-party API and through cloud platforms (e.g. Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and other partner offerings). In practice the customer's existing cloud, identity system and procurement decide which one you target. Check feature availability per platform (e.g. the Files API is not on Bedrock or Vertex; beta features vary).

Identity and data residency matter for security. Use the platform's native identity (IAM roles, workload identity) rather than long-lived keys where possible, and pin the region to the approved geography.

Pin the version so an upstream change isn't a silent production change. An alias (a name that moves to the latest snapshot) means that when the provider updates it, your production behaviour, cost and latency change without a deploy. Reference an explicit dated snapshot instead:

model = "claude-sonnet-latest"        # moving alias: the first line follows a moving target
model = "claude-sonnet-<dated-snapshot>"   # pinned: the second line pins the snapshot

Promote a version through the eval. To adopt a new snapshot, run your eval suite against it, compare to the current version, adapt prompts, shadow or canary, then switch — keeping the previous version deployable for rollback. Pinning, retaining prior versions and gating promotion on the eval add release-process overhead to every deployment; that overhead is the price of reviewable migration and fast rollback.

The deployment that broke when the alias moved. A service used a moving alias; after an upstream update, outputs shifted and a downstream parser broke, with no eval gate and no quick rollback. The root cause was a silent production change.

Comparing platforms so the choice survives review.

  • Latency: measure from the customer's region, not your laptop.
  • Compliance: often determines the platform outright (residency, certifications, BAA/ FedRAMP routes).
  • Total cost beyond the per-token rate: data transfer, support plan, committed spend, private networking, operations overhead. Measure all three per platform so a procurement team will sign off; the platform picked on familiarity that failed residency is the cautionary example.

Real life. Writing "Python 3.12" in the lockfile instead of "latest", and keeping last month's build in the garage.

Tech. Pinned container image digests with a rollback tag.

notes.title: Trust boundaries
notes.html:
Coordinating several Claude deployments. A multi-component application (retriever, agent, ticketing system, other Claude deployments) has components that each do a different thing and pass data between them. Map which component does what before you connect them.

The trust boundary is where data moves. Every seam between components is a place where data crosses from one trust level to another: untrusted content entering the agent, model output flowing into a system of record, a customer's data entering a shared service. The unmarked seam is where reviews stall and incidents start (in the pairing-session story, the seam nobody marked as a boundary was identified only at the end of an exchange).

Rules.

  1. Name every seam as a trust boundary.
  2. Least privilege applies to the whole application: each component gets its own scoped credential and the minimum access it needs.
  3. Controls at each boundary: validation of what crosses, authorization, output handling.
  4. Log boundary crossings so a review has an audit trail.
  5. Scope for a regulated review: the multi-component map is what pulls the module together (identity, secrets, residency, logging, injection defence) into something deployable.

The integration map. A diagram or table listing components, what each can read/write, which credential it uses, where data is stored, which region, and what is logged at each hop. Include it in the design document.

Cost. Mapping seams, enforcing controls at each and logging crossings adds design and audit work to every integration; skipping it is what stalls the review.

Real life. Border crossings between countries: each has a checkpoint and a log.

Tech. Service-mesh mTLS and per-service IAM roles.

notes.title: Packaging and contributing
notes.html:
Packaging a working build so the next engagement starts from an asset. An accelerator keeps the reusable parts and separates out the customer-specific ones, so a delivery becomes something the next engagement configures in hours instead of rebuilds from scratch.

Asset types package differently (e.g. prompt/skill libraries, eval suites, MCP server configs, plugins, infrastructure templates, reference architectures, runbooks). The checklist per asset: what is reusable, what is parameterized, what is customer-specific, what assumptions it makes, how it's tested.

What correct packaging requires.

  • Parameterize while the build is fresh: turning customer values into configuration (names, endpoints, regions, keys-by-reference) is cheapest now and expensive later.
  • Separate generalizable from customer-specific parts.
  • Document both the code and the assumptions (what must be true for the asset to work).
  • Bundle the audit log / evidence as part of the package where compliance matters.
  • Accept that separating and documenting adds real time to the first build; the payoff comes on reuse.
  • Cautionary tale: "the template that shipped fast and couldn't be reused" — hard-coded customer details and undocumented assumptions made it worthless to the next team.

Moving an asset into shared infrastructure. Contributing upstream (an open-source library, a marketplace, a shared repository a maintainer accepts):

  1. Match the contribution to the channel built for it (issue, PR, plugin marketplace, docs).
  2. Make verification possible: working examples and tests a maintainer can run; a clear description of behaviour.
  3. Rights and attribution come before technical review: confirm you own or may license the code, respect licences of any dependencies and customer data in examples, and give proper attribution — otherwise the PR stalls regardless of code quality.
  4. Clear the maintainer bar and the licensing gate; this is real work on top of making the code run for you.
  5. Cautionary tale: the pull request a maintainer couldn't verify (no examples, no tests, unclear rights).

Real life. Turning a one-off recipe into a franchise manual: ingredients parameterized, steps documented, a taste test included.

Tech. Extracting a library from a client project and getting a pull request merged upstream.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Constraints pick the route. Privilege: direct API/SDK in the firm's app, SSO, approved gateway, application-layer logging (Anthropic doesn't capture content by default). HIPAA: BAA-covered configuration only (HIPAA-enabled org via Anthropic or Bedrock/Vertex on eligible account); BAA excludes Console, Workbench, beta features, consumer plans. GDPR/EU: Bedrock/Vertex with pinned region (direct API has no EU residency). FedRAMP: Claude for Government, Bedrock GovCloud, Vertex Assured Workloads — Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is not authorized; keep dev/test off the commercial endpoint; verify at trust.anthropic.com. Internal policy: use the CIO-cleared client. Managed Agents out for PHI/ZDR.

Requirements and lifecycle. Functional then infrastructure requirements before choosing a platform; document for defensibility; lifecycle phases each with artifact and gate; skipping gates is the failure.

Platforms and pinning. Customer's cloud usually decides; compare latency from the customer's region, compliance, total cost; pin dated snapshots (aliases move); promote through the eval; keep the prior version for rollback; check per-platform feature availability.

Trust boundaries. Map components; every seam is a boundary; least privilege per component with its own credential; controls and logging at crossings; integration map in the design doc.

Packaging and contributing. Accelerators: parameterize early, separate customer-specific parts, document assumptions, bundle audit evidence. Upstream: right channel, examples + tests, rights/licensing/attribution first.

One-liners.

  • "The governing constraint picks the endpoint before the prompt is written."
  • "Pin the snapshot; promote through the eval."
  • "Name every seam as a trust boundary."
  • "Parameterize while the build is fresh."

questions.promptHtml:
A client sends PHI to Claude. Which setup is acceptable?

  • A. Console/Workbench for convenience
  • B. A BAA-covered configuration (direct API on a HIPAA-enabled org arranged with Anthropic, or Bedrock/Vertex on the partner's HIPAA-eligible account), with logging paths scoped under the same BAA
  • C. A beta feature under the BAA
  • D. Consumer plan with a policy memo

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The BAA does not cover Console, Workbench, beta features or consumer plans; verify feature eligibility.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: PHI may only go to a BAA-covered configuration: a dedicated HIPAA-enabled Anthropic organization (arranged with Anthropic) or Bedrock/Vertex on the partner's HIPAA-eligible account. Any logging or retention path you write to must be scoped under the same BAA. Console, Workbench, beta features and consumer plans are not covered; not every API feature is eligible.

questions.promptHtml:
An EU customer needs data processed only in-region. What is the right route?

  • A. The direct Anthropic API with its default endpoint
  • B. Bedrock or Vertex with the region pinned in client configuration (the direct API does not currently provide EU data residency)
  • C. A global endpoint
  • D. Any region, since data is encrypted

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Defaulting to a global endpoint without a region is the common failure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Residency must be enforceable in code: pin the region in the client configuration for a covered jurisdiction. The direct Anthropic API does not currently provide EU data residency, and a global endpoint can serve a request from outside the boundary. Encryption (D) does not change where processing happens.

questions.promptHtml:
Which is NOT an authorized FedRAMP route in the source material?

  • A. Claude for Government (FedRAMP High via PFCS-SS)
  • B. Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud (High, DoD IL4/5)
  • C. Claude via Vertex AI Assured Workloads
  • D. Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: D. Also keep dev/test off the commercial endpoint, since code patterns and credentials leak between environments.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Verify current status at trust.anthropic.com.

questions.promptHtml:
A law firm needs privileged documents processed. What survives review?

  • A. Consumer Claude.ai
  • B. Direct API/SDK calls from the firm's own app via SSO and an approved LLM gateway with full request/response logging implemented at the application layer
  • C. Any endpoint, if the prompt says "confidential"
  • D. Personal API keys

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Conversation content is not captured by Anthropic by default on direct API traffic, so you must log it; confirm the design with the account team.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The firm needs an audited path: direct API or SDK calls from its own application, SSO, an approved LLM gateway, and full request and response logging. Because Anthropic does not capture conversation content by default on direct API traffic, the organization must implement the logging itself. Consumer surfaces cannot be audited end to end, and a prompt wording does not change the endpoint.

questions.contextHtml: A production service called the model through a moving alias. After an upstream update, outputs shifted and a downstream parser broke. There was no eval run and no way to roll back quickly.
questions.promptHtml:
What should the release process include?

  • A. Always use the newest alias
  • B. Pin a model snapshot, promote a new version only through the eval, and retain the prior version for rollback
  • C. Test manually
  • D. Avoid upgrades forever

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blaming the vendor for the change.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in outputs? Which eval cases regressed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin the last known good snapshot.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Alias moved; prompt sensitivity; parser brittleness.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the eval against both versions.
  5. Root cause: A silent production change via an unpinned alias.
  6. Fix: B.
  7. Prevention: Gate promotion on eval scores; keep the previous version deployable.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Pinning adds release overhead; accept it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Which platform? → Usually the customer's cloud; compare latency from their region, compliance and total cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the vendor.
  • Hire: pins.
  • Strong hire: pins, gates on eval, retains rollback.

questions.promptHtml:
What comes before choosing a platform?

  • A. Buying credits
  • B. Deriving checkable functional and infrastructure requirements from the business problem and documenting them so the decision can be defended
  • C. Writing the UI
  • D. Picking the biggest model

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Each lifecycle phase should have an artifact and a gate; skipping gates under deadline is the usual failure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Capture functional requirements from the business problem, then derive infrastructure requirements (residency, identity, latency, volume) before any platform is picked, and document them so the decision is defensible. Each lifecycle phase needs a defined artifact and a gate; gates are what teams under deadline are tempted to skip.

questions.contextHtml: A multi-component Claude application passes data between a retriever, an agent, and a ticketing system. Nobody marked the hand-off between retriever and agent as a boundary; a review stalls.
questions.promptHtml:
What do you do?

  • A. Nothing; internal hops are trusted
  • B. Map components, name every seam as a trust boundary, apply least privilege per component and log boundary crossings
  • C. Merge everything into one component
  • D. Remove logging

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Assuming internal hops are safe.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What data crosses each seam? Who can write to it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add logging at the seams.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Unvalidated content enters the agent; over-broad credentials.
  4. How I'd verify each: Walk the integration map.
  5. Root cause: An unnamed seam.
  6. Fix: B.
  7. Prevention: Include the map in the design doc.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't skip audit work to save time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Who owns the credential for each component? → Each gets its own, scoped narrowly.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: trusts internal hops.
  • Hire: names boundaries.
  • Strong hire: boundaries plus least privilege plus logging.

questions.promptHtml:
How do you turn a one-off delivery into a reusable asset?

  • A. Zip the repo
  • B. Parameterize while the build is fresh, separate customer-specific from reusable parts, document assumptions and bundle the audit log
  • C. Delete tests
  • D. Hard-code the customer name

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Contributing upstream additionally needs verifiable examples and tests plus a rights/licensing/attribution check before technical review.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: An accelerator keeps reusable parts and separates customer-specific ones while the build is fresh, documents assumptions, and bundles the audit log. To contribute upstream, match the contribution to the right channel, include examples and tests a maintainer can verify, and clear rights, licensing and attribution first.
